acceptable_visual_variants: A classic wooden shehnai with a polished brass bell.
A shehnai resting on a decorative silk cloth alongside wedding or festive motifs.
cultural_entities.gloss: A traditional South Asian double-reed oboe-like wind instrument, deeply associated with weddings, celebrations, and auspicious beginnings. In this poetic context, it symbolizes the celebratory and joyous music of dreams.
negative_confusions: A modern brass trumpet or saxophone.
cultural_entities.translation_note: The translation replaces the specific South Asian wind instrument 'shehnai' with the generic concept of 'melody'.
visual_features: A long, conical wooden instrument with a brass or metal bell at the end.
Multiple finger holes along the body.
Often decorated with red or gold tassels or threads during festive occasions.

annotation.emotional_arc: A complex oscillation between intense desire to live and a dramatic readiness to die, resolving into a deep appreciation of fleeting moments.

stanzas.loss_note: The translation of 'shehnai' as 'melody' loses the specific cultural association of the shehnai instrument with celebration, weddings, and auspicious beginnings.

metaphor_spans.abstract_meaning: The joyful, celebratory, and musical feeling of having hopeful dreams and desires.

translation_loss.what_was_lost: The specific cultural and celebratory associations of the 'shehnai' (शहनाई), a traditional South Asian wind instrument played at weddings and auspicious occasions, are flattened into the generic English word 'melody'.

The Urdu-derived poetic resonance of 'tamanna' (desire/longing), 'irada' (intent/resolve), and 'aabaad' (prosperous/flourishing/populated) is lost in the standard English translation, which uses more clinical or generic terms like 'want', 'intent', and 'flourishing'.

stanzas.loss_note: The rhythmic and grammatical parallelism of 'jinhe jeena hai, jinme jeena hai' is slightly flattened in English, though the semantic meaning is preserved.

translation_loss.what_was_lost: The rhythmic parallel structure and internal rhyme of 'jinhein jeena hai, jinmein jeena hai' (which to live, in which to live) is grammatically accurate in translation but loses its lyrical, song-like cadence and poetic flow.

annotation.theme: The intense, contradictory fullness of human emotion where the desire to live fully and the willingness to die coexist.

original_poem:
आज फिर जीने की तमन्ना है,  
आज फिर मरने का इरादा है।  
आज फिर ख्वाबों की शहनाई है,  
आज फिर दिल की दुनिया आबाद है।  

कितनी बातें हैं, कितने लम्हे हैं,  
जिन्हें जीना है, जिनमें जीना है।  
आज फिर जीने की तमन्ना है,  
आज फिर मरने का इरादा है।
poem_title: Aaj Phir Jeene Ki Tamanna Hai
translated_poem:
Today again I want to live,  
Today again I have the intent to die.  
Today again there’s the melody of dreams,  
Today again the world of my heart is flourishing.  

There are so many things, so many moments,  
Which I want to live, in which I want to live.  
Today again I want to live,  
Today again I have the intent to die.
